reason: The cited evidence (E1, E2) supports twinning-induced work hardening in dual-phase HEAs under monotonic loading at low temperatures, but provides no data on creep, sustained stress, or engineered interfaces. The key premises linking twinning barriers to creep resistance and the design of such interfaces are unsupported by the cited passages. E3 is listed as conflicting but is not used to support the premises.
premises: Deformation twinning in the FCC phase of dual-phase HEAs increases work hardening at room and cryogenic temperatures.
Engineered FCC/BCC interfaces can be designed to restrict dislocation motion and trigger localized deformation twinning.
Localized deformation twinning at interfaces acts as an intrinsic barrier to dislocation motion, delaying creep.
The proposed dual mechanism (dislocation pile-up + twinning) impedes continuous plastic flow required for steady-state creep.
The beneficial effect operates under sustained stress and moderate-to-high temperatures typical of service conditions.
